name: potrace
why: Turning bitmaps into clean vector outlines is a satisfying transform that shows how tracing actually works.

brief.what_it_is: Potrace is a command-line tool that traces a bitmap and turns it into a smooth, scalable vector image. It takes bitmap input in PBM, PGM, PPM, or BMP format. It writes one of several vector formats: SVG, PDF, EPS, PostScript, DXF, GeoJSON, PGM (for antialiasing pixel images), Gimppath, or XFig. A companion program, mkbitmap, is distributed with it to pre-process greyscale and colour images before tracing.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to get clean, resolution-independent images from scanned or pixel-based sources, such as company or university logos and handwritten notes. The author says the result is 'not "jaggy" like a bitmap, but smooth.'
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the algorithm in detail; it links to a separate technical PDF that I did not open. The listed options hint at the steps: a turd-size filter removes speckles, an alphamax corner threshold decides where corners stay sharp, a curve-optimization tolerance simplifies curves, and a turn policy resolves ambiguities when decomposing paths.

commands_seen.context: Debian and Ubuntu install, per the package-management footnote on the homepage.

Usage synopsis from the built-in help text. Options include -b for backend selection, -t for speckle size, -a for corner threshold, and -s for SVG output.

brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no Homebrew-specific steps. Source builds use the standard configure and make commands, with options described in the INSTALL and README files shipped with the source. Windows has 32-bit and 64-bit zips, installers, and a README-WIN. Precompiled tarballs exist for Mac OS X (64-bit), Linux, and several BSD and Unix systems. Most Linux distributions and BSD ports carry it as a package. The tool needs no account, runtime, or first-run configuration.
brief.standout: It has been the standard open-source bitmap tracer for many years, and its output is smooth Bézier curves rather than the jagged traces of simpler tools. The homepage's downstream list is unusually broad, covering FontForge, Inkscape, LilyPond via mftrace, stained-glass and stencil projects, and ports in more than a dozen languages.
brief.status: Quiet. The latest release listed on the homepage is 1.16, dated September 17, 2019, and the version section also says 1.16. The news section has no entries after 2019. Some third-party entries on the page are dated 2021 and 2026, but I found no new Potrace release after 2019.
brief.caveats: Input is limited to PNM (PBM, PGM, PPM) and BMP, and the homepage gives no colour tracing. Vector Magic is named as the commercial option that handles colour. Potrace is GPL-licensed. The name 'Potrace' is a trademark of the author, Peter Selinger, so ports need his permission to use it. A non-GPL version, Potrace Professional, is sold by Icosasoft under dual licensing. Some Solaris and FreeBSD binaries are dated 1.15 rather than 1.16.
quotes: Potrace(TM) is a tool for tracing a bitmap, which means, transforming a bitmap into a smooth, scalable image.
The resulting image is not "jaggy" like a bitmap, but smooth. It can then be rendered at any resolution.
I particularly love projects that use Potrace to create objects in the physical world, such as C. Scott Ananian's article on how to make stained glass windows from color scans

judge.reason: Potrace turns pixels into optimized Bézier paths, making a familiar image transformation tangible through a distinctive, long-standing tracing tool.

entry.title: potrace
entry.tldr: Potrace traces a bitmap and turns it into smooth, scalable vector curves, the tracer behind much of the open-source graphics world.
entry.deeper_look:
Potrace reads a bitmap (PBM, PGM, PPM or BMP) and writes a vector image: SVG, PDF, EPS, PostScript, DXF, GeoJSON, XFig and a few others. The pixel edges become smooth Bézier curves, so the result can be rendered at any resolution. In the author's words, the result is "not "jaggy" like a bitmap, but smooth."

It exists for jobs like rescuing a scanned logo or handwritten notes from the resolution it was scanned at. A companion program, mkbitmap, ships with it. It pre-processes greyscale and colour images into the black-and-white input that potrace wants.

The options hint at how tracing works. A turd-size filter drops speckles, an alphamax threshold decides which corners stay sharp, a curve-optimization tolerance simplifies the curves, and a turn policy settles ambiguous spots when the bitmap is split into paths. Tuning them shows what "tracing" actually decides on your behalf. The homepage links a separate technical write-up of the algorithm.

The homepage lists downstream projects, including FontForge, Inkscape, and LilyPond via mftrace. It also lists physical-world uses such as stained glass and stencils.

Shows the options of the companion tool that turns greyscale or colour images into traceable bitmaps.
The usage synopsis. Give it a PBM, PGM, PPM or BMP file and pick a backend, such as -s for SVG output, to get a vector file.

entry.whats_unique: It has been the standard open-source bitmap tracer for years, and it produces smooth Bézier curves rather than jagged traces. Its ecosystem of ports and downstream projects is unusually broad.
entry.caveats: Input is limited to PNM and BMP, there is no colour tracing, and the last release (1.16) dates from September 2019.
